title: Sources close
hook: seventy days as a guest in many houses
tomorrow: next, the poets. why did Rumi sign his poems with another name?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine's garden: take up and read. My companion text. Today the reading closes, and it's time to say thank you on the way out the door.
screen: `MY COMPANION TEXT.` → `ON THE WAY OUT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: After a dinner party, there are two kinds of rides home. In one, you talk about how much work went into it. In the other, you pick it apart. The Talmud quotes Ben Zoma, the sage who blessed the crowd on the Temple Mount, and he noticed the same two guests. The good guest, he says, talks like this: look how much trouble my host went to for me. All that meat, all that wine, all those cakes. And all the trouble he took, he took just for me.
screen: `TWO RIDES HOME.` → `BEN ZOMA'S TWO GUESTS.` → `ALL THIS TROUBLE, FOR ME.`

segments.voice: The bad guest says: what trouble? I ate one piece of bread, drank one cup. Whatever he did, he did for his own family. Same table, same food. The only difference is what the guest notices. Here's the teaching, and it's lived, not only told. Jewish grace after meals, Birkat Hamazon, said after a meal with bread, has a line where the guest asks God to bless the master of this house. The Talmud even records a guest's blessing for the host: that he not be put to shame, in this world or the next. Gratitude, in this tradition, isn't a feeling you wait for. It's a sentence you say at the table, naming the host. Now this path's seventy days. You've been a guest in many houses: Buddhist, Jewish, Christian, Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, Confucian. Those books came to you from people who chanted them, copied them and kept them, long before you opened them. A good guest says: look at the trouble they took, and I got a seat at the table. One to tell a friend tonight: in the Talmud, the good guest and the bad guest ate exactly the same meal.
screen: `THE BAD GUEST: WHAT TROUBLE?` · `A BLESSING FOR THE MASTER OF THE HOUSE.` · `GRATITUDE IS A SENTENCE.` · `MANY HOUSES, ONE GOOD GUEST.` · then, large: `THANK THE HOSTS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who hosted you lately, at a table, a couch or a long talk. Send them a short text that names one thing they did, the way the good guest names the meat and the wine. Then, quietly, thank the people who kept one book from this shelf: monks, scribes, teachers, families at a table.
Sources close: seventy days as a guest in many houses, and the thank-you at the door.
Your line: thank the hosts. Name what they did, the way the good guest does. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Birkat Hamazon, the Jewish grace after meals, includes a request that God bless the host when a guest leads it; Ben Zoma's good and bad guest (Berakhot 58a) is a teaching on noticing what the host has done.

chat.says: dinner at ray's new place. he cooked with his shaky hands. how do i thank him without it being weird
options: Like Ben Zoma's good guest: name the trouble he took, the dish, the effort, for you.
Bring a gift worth the same as dinner, so you're even and owe him nothing.
Don't mention it. A good guest never draws attention to the host's effort.
chat.meaning: Ben Zoma's good guest says: look at the trouble my host took, just for me. Gratitude names the host's effort out loud.
